title: Loot
synopsis: Your husband cheated. The divorce settlement gave you eighty-seven billion dollars. Your foundation has a staff of six and a board of one — you — and you don't know what an audit is. Start there.

nodes.text: You arrive at the Wells Foundation at noon in three-day-old yacht clothes. Sofia, your director, hands you a coffee that you don't recognize as coffee. The whiteboard has goals on it.

choices.text: Pretend you already know everything
choices.consequence: Confidence is a kind of competence.

choices.text: Ask Sofia to walk you through everything

nodes.text: Sofia has booked you on three morning shows. You will be asked how it feels to give away a fortune. You realize on the limo ride that you have no answer that isn't 'great?'

choices.text: Wing it and hope you sound human
Pre-write three honest sentences

nodes.text: Howard is the foundation's accountant and is, you discover, extremely fun once he stops being terrified of you. He shows you the line items. You ask, sincerely, what 'overhead' is.

choices.text: Make Howard your real guide
choices.consequence: Numbers people are also feelings people.

choices.text: Buy Howard a better office chair first

nodes.text: Sofia takes you to a shelter the foundation funds. The director recognizes the foundation but not you. She gives you the same tour she gives any donor. You realize you have been invisible to the shelter your money built.

choices.text: Tell her who you are
choices.consequence: You commit to “Tell her who you are.” The story records the instinct as “Take ownership” and carries it forward.

choices.text: Stay anonymous, observe

nodes.text: An old yacht photo of you holding a glass of champagne with caption 'rough day' goes viral the morning after a flood in Mississippi. Sofia's phone is making a sound she has never heard it make.

choices.text: Apologize in your own words on camera
Donate aggressively to the flood relief

nodes.text: Your driver Nicholas is also your son-from-a-first-marriage's age and an aspiring actor and the only person who tells you the truth this week. You realize you've been treating him as scenery.

choices.text: Promote Nicholas to assistant
Pay for his class and keep him driving
choices.consequence: Don't trap him in your gratitude.

nodes.text: Arthur, fifty, divorced, runs operations and treats you with the patient kindness of a man who has, you sense, seen many billionaires miss the point. You like him. He scares you a little. You decide to listen.

choices.text: Ask Arthur to be your sponsor at the foundation
Date Arthur for one bad month

nodes.text: Your ex-husband John, the tech billionaire who detonated your marriage, calls. He's been to therapy. He wants to apologize. He may also want, very gently, to know what you're doing with the money.

choices.text: Take the apology, refuse the conversation
Hear him out — over the phone, not in person
choices.consequence: Curiosity is allowed; proximity, less so.

nodes.text: You and your assistant Rhonda go to Vegas for the weekend and spend ninety thousand dollars on a slot machine and a hat. Sofia calls. You answer in a casino bathroom. You realize, slowly, that you might be self-sabotaging.

choices.text: Call your therapist on the way home
Donate ten million the next morning to compensate
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Performative penance—follows you into whatever comes next.

nodes.text: You finally ask to be added to the actual decision-making board. Sofia is surprised. Arthur is, secretly, delighted. You sit through your first vote on a hundred-million-dollar housing initiative. You actually understand most of it.

choices.text: Vote yes and learn from the consequences
Vote present and ask better questions
choices.consequence: Don't be the loudest person in your own building.

nodes.text: You realize that Sofia, terrifyingly, has become your closest friend — and that you have not been a great friend back. You ask her to dinner that is not work. You ask about her sister, who you've never met but somehow know about.

choices.text: Show up at Sofia's family event this weekend
Send a thoughtful thing instead
choices.consequence: Don't impose your money on her life.

nodes.text: After six months you realize the foundation's mission, on paper, is too vague. You propose a sharper one: end family homelessness in two states inside ten years. Sofia stares at you. Arthur smiles.

choices.text: Push the new mission to the board
choices.consequence: You let the choice stand. The path shifts almost imperceptibly, marked by one lasting impulse: Aim, big.

choices.text: Pilot it in one city first

nodes.text: You promote Howard out of accounting and into program strategy. He is briefly stunned. He brings you a binder the next morning with twenty-eight slides he made over the weekend. The first one is titled 'Where the Money Could Actually Go.'

choices.text: Adopt half his slides immediately
Make him present to the board next Tuesday

nodes.text: John shows up unannounced at your gate at midnight. He's drunk. He wants to talk. He is, on close inspection, the man you married and not the man you became with him.

choices.text: Send him home in his own car
choices.consequence: Goodbye sometimes is the kindest verb.

choices.text: Talk to him for one hour, then send him home

nodes.text: The foundation's first annual gala under the new mission. You are giving the speech. You have written and unwritten it eleven times. Arthur is in the second row trying to look professional.

choices.text: Throw out the speech and speak honestly
Stick to the script and let the room cry

nodes.text: The mission is, in the first two cities, working — slowly, imperfectly, more than anyone expected. The foundation has hired sharper than it ever did under any director. You have learned to read a 10-K. You hate it less than you thought.

choices.text: Stay engaged for another decade
choices.consequence: This is the life you got, late.

choices.text: Bring on a President so you can step back

nodes.text: Arthur, over a pizza in your absurd kitchen, tells you he likes you. He also tells you he doesn't want to date you. He wants to be a real friend for a long time. You discover, surprisingly, that this is exactly the right offer.

choices.text: Accept it as the gift it is
Hold out for romance and lose the friendship
choices.consequence: Sometimes wanting more loses what you have.

nodes.text: You write John a letter you never send. It thanks him, in a strange way, for leaving you. The money was the engine of an entire life you had been postponing. Forgiveness is the strangest dividend.

choices.text: Burn the letter; keep the lesson
choices.consequence: Some closure is for you alone.

choices.text: Donate ten million in his name to spite him

nodes.text: Sunday. Sofia stops by with coffee and the paper. You sit on a porch you built with foundation money and decide, slowly, whether the next chapter is interior or public. Both, you realize, are real options now.

choices.text: Keep the next chapter inward
Channel the energy outward, even pettily

nodes.text: Family homelessness is down 38% in your two pilot states. The data is real. The headlines are mostly accurate. Sofia is on the cover of a magazine you never read. You are, finally, very proud of something that is not your hair.

choices.text: Take the second decade — scale the mission
choices.consequence: Don't stop because you finished one chapter.

choices.text: Hand off and become a private donor with opinions

nodes.text: You find, in your fifties, the version of you that John didn't get to ruin. You like her. She buys good wine. She also funds, quietly, a scholarship called 'For the Late Bloomers.' You laugh every time you sign the check.
The donation in John's name funds, accidentally, the program that ends up beating his own foundation's outcomes by every metric. He calls to congratulate you. You let it go to voicemail. You smile.

You sign on for another decade. The mission scales to nine states. Sofia opens a London office. You buy Arthur a really good chair. Howard goes back to overhead accounting because he missed it. Everyone, you realize, is good at exactly the thing they fled and returned to.

You step back. Sofia becomes President. You become the eccentric who shows up to galas in a hat and writes one careful editorial a year. The foundation outgrows you. That, you realize, is what foundations are for.
